slides.title: Stage-1 Calibration: Procurement and Build
slides.subtitle: The sphere, board and fixtures needed for the depth-sensor calibration captures
slides.notes: This is the first of two decks on the stage-1 calibration captures. It covers what has to be bought and made before a capture session: one matte sphere, a flat board, their mountings on the robot flange, and a three-ball nest, with estimated costs and candidate suppliers. The second deck covers the test procedure itself and what the robot program must do. Both are summaries of the stage-1 capture procedure in docs/procedures, whose section 3a and appendix A hold the full build details.

slides.title: One sphere and a board carry the known geometry
slides.caption: Sphere on its stem, side view: the stem points away from the sensor so that the sphere hides it.

cards.head: Sphere B
cards.text: 152.4 mm diameter, turned aluminum, matte; the only sphere

cards.head: Curvature sweep
cards.text: Nine stations from 300 to 1,100 mm, each about 1.19 times farther than the last

cards.head: Board
cards.text: 200 x 150 mm, at least 6 mm thick, flat to 0.05 mm after painting; tilted 0, 20 and 40 degrees

slides.notes: The calibration compares what the sensor measures with targets of known shape held at known poses by the robot. The sensor averages depth over a patch of pixels, and on a curved surface that averaging biases the depth by an amount that depends on how curved the surface looks per pixel, not on its physical radius alone. Moving one sphere from 300 to 1,100 mm changes that apparent curvature more than thirteenfold, so one sphere swept through the volume measures the effect; a second, smaller sphere is no longer needed (decision D-15 of the analysis). What is given up is the cross-check two radii would give, that a small sphere near the sensor and a large one twice as far away show the same bias. The larger sphere is kept because it still covers enough pixels at 1,100 mm. The board supplies zero curvature and controlled tilts. A sphere's orientation does not matter, only its center, which is why the mounting must hold the center fixed rather than aim the sphere precisely.

slides.title: What must be built

rows: Sphere-flange mount: adapter plate and stem
Run-out fixture: dial indicator on a magnetic base and steel base plate

slides.caption: Section 1b of the procedure; nothing outside sections 1a to 1f is needed for a session.
slides.notes: This is the complete list of apparatus to build before the first session, as section 1b of the procedure gives it. Each purchase order asks the fabricator for an inspection report of the toleranced features on the drawing; those reports are the as-built record. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-02 adapter plate, SC1-04 stem with the sphere interface, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base (SC1-01 and SC1-03, for the former second sphere, are archived). The rigid sensor mount is built from the existing drawing from previous work. The run-out fixture needs no drawing: it is a bought dial indicator on a bought magnetic base, standing on a plain steel plate bolted to the table. Everything already in hand, everything to buy and the preparation tasks are on the following slides and in sections 1a, 1c and 1f.

slides.title: What must be bought

rows: Outside micrometer 150-175 mm, with setting standard
Rough TCP length; board distance D; board size
Thread locker, retaining compound, shims, alcohol, padded case

slides.caption: A phone camera is enough for the setup photos. Already in hand: sensor, robot, capture computer with its communication software, analysis computer.
slides.notes: These are the tools and consumables, section 1c of the procedure. One outside micrometer, 150 to 175 mm, replaces any laboratory measurement: the sphere's diameter is measured in-house after the matte finish, at six or more orientations, and the spread of the readings doubles as the sphericity check. It comes with a setting standard, used to check it before each measurement. The straightedge with a 0.05 mm feeler leaf checks the board's flatness after painting and after mounting; the run-out on the robot checks only that the face is square to the flange, not that it is flat. These, the calipers for the board's size and the nest re-seat check are the only in-house checks; everything else is in the fabricators' inspection reports. Items already in hand are the sensor, the robot, the capture computer with its communication software, which also takes the capture trigger from the robot, and the analysis computer.

slides.title: Building and buying cost about $1,875 to $5,150

Run-out fixture: dial indicator, magnetic base, steel base plate

stats.label: aluminum sphere B turned by a job shop, tools included
sphere B made to order, tools included

slides.caption: Tools and consumables $485 to $1,130, included in the totals. Estimates of October 2026, plus or minus 50 percent; sphere B is the least certain.
slides.notes: These estimates come from suppliers' list prices where they exist and from typical job-shop rates of about 80 to 150 dollars an hour otherwise. With one sphere, one adapter plate, one stem and one micrometer are needed. The sphere figure includes no laboratory measurement: the diameter is measured in-house with the micrometer on the buy list. The two totals differ only in the sphere: turned in aluminum by a job shop with the thread cut in, against made to order by a ball or ceramics maker. The fabricators' inspection reports may carry a fee; ask for it in each quote. The rigid sensor mount is built from an existing drawing and is not estimated here. Quotes are needed before ordering.

slides.title: Purchase specification: the target sphere

rows: Known to 0.025 mm, by micrometer at six or more orientations after finishing, at the session's room temperature
Turned aluminum (6061-T6), solid or hollow with at least 6 mm wall; ceramic as an alternative
Matte hard anodize, light gray or natural, uniform, free of highlights
M20 x 30 mm tapped hole at a pole, 32 mm spot face, cut when the sphere is turned
The turner's inspection report: diameter and sphericity as turned, thread and spot face

slides.caption: Procedure section 1d; drawing SC1-04 shows the interface.
slides.notes: This is the purchase specification of section 1d of the procedure, to hand to the shop that turns the sphere. The name sphere B is kept because the drawings and the related projects use it. The diameter requirement is decision D-13: known to 0.025 mm after the matte finish, measured in-house with the outside micrometer; the mean of six or more readings goes in the pose log, and their spread checks the 0.02 mm sphericity. Aluminum grows 0.0035 mm in diameter per degree C at this size, so it is measured at the temperature of the session. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-02 adapter plate, SC1-04 stem with the sphere interface, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base (SC1-01 and SC1-03, for the former second sphere, are archived).

slides.title: Purchase specification: flat plate

rows: 200 x 150 mm, at least 6 mm thick
Finish-ground aluminum tooling plate (for example MIC-6) or float glass
0.05 mm over the front face, checked with a straightedge and a 0.05 mm feeler leaf after painting and after mounting
Thin, even matte light-gray paint; do not bead-blast a plate thinner than about 10 mm
Bottom long edge and left short edge square and clean: they rest on the adapter's edge pins
Supplier's flatness report, kept with the session notes

slides.caption: Procedure section 1d; the board outline is on drawing SC1-05.
slides.notes: The board is checked flat after painting and after mounting because that is the state the sensor sees, and the flatness report is the reference for the board-flatness check in the validation. A 6 mm plate sags only about 0.002 mm under its own weight, so thickness is a matter of surviving the finish and the mounting, not stiffness. The bottom and left edges locate the board against the three edge pins of the board adapter, which centers it on the flange axis. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-02 adapter plate, SC1-04 stem with the sphere interface, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base (SC1-01 and SC1-03, for the former second sphere, are archived).

slides.title: The sphere must be matte and measured, not certified

columns.head: Finish
points: Matte hard anodize on the turned aluminum sphere
A mirror sphere is unusable: one bright highlight
Steel or ceramic alternative: bead-blast with fine glass bead
Matte paint is the last resort: 0.02 to 0.05 mm per coat

columns.head: Diameter
points: Known to 0.025 mm, measured after the finish
Measured in-house by outside micrometer at six or more orientations
Aluminum grows 0.0035 mm per degree C: measure at session temperature
The mean goes in the pose log; the spread checks sphericity

columns.head: Mounting
points: M20 thread cut at the pole when the sphere is turned
Hardened steel or ceramic cannot be tapped
Alternative: blind hole 16 H7 x 46 mm, stem bonded
No tapped 6 inch precision sphere is stocked

slides.notes: A mirror finish returns one bright highlight from the sensor's projector and almost nothing else, so the sphere must be matte; the hard anodize of the aluminum sphere gives that directly. The diameter requirement is decision D-13: known to 0.025 mm after finishing, which is a radius error of about 0.0125 mm, an eighth of the target at 500 mm; no maker's certificate is needed. The diameter is measured in-house with the outside micrometer. Only if the sphere is bought in steel or ceramic does the alternative mounting apply: such spheres are hardened and cannot be tapped, so they get a bonded stem.

slides.title: Candidate suppliers

rows: Precision turning shop (aluminum); Bal-tec; RGP Balls; Industrial Tectonics; Morgan Advanced Materials
A 6 inch matte sphere with a mounting hole is a custom item
Laser-scanner spheres, Rothbucher RSLB10M among them
Not usable: form errors of 0.3 to 2 mm
McMaster-Carr MIC-6 plus a grinding shop; Edmund Optics float glass
Painted matte after grinding; flatness checked after mounting
Adapter, stem, board adapter, nest base
Inspection report of the toleranced features on each order
Outside micrometer 150-175 mm: Mitutoyo 103-143-10, or Starrett
In-house, after the matte finish; setting standard included
Mitutoyo 2046 series; Noga MG71003 or DG-61003

slides.caption: From suppliers' web pages, October 2026; not an endorsement. Confirm size, finish, measurement and thread before ordering.
slides.notes: This list is appendix A of the procedure in brief. No supplier was found that stocks a precision 6 inch sphere with a mounting hole, so the sphere is either turned in aluminum with the thread cut in, or made to order by a ball or ceramics maker. The laser-scanner reference spheres sold near this size have form errors of 0.3 to 2 mm; the Rothbucher sphere is the best specified of them, and even it is too coarse now that one sphere must serve near range too, where the depth-scaled target is 0.04 to 0.1 mm. The finished diameter is measured in-house with the outside micrometer, which is cheaper than buying a certified sphere and is what the calibration actually needs.

slides.title: Run-out fixture: dial indicator and its mounting

cards.head: Dial indicator
cards.text: 0.01 mm graduation, about 10 mm travel; for example Mitutoyo 2046 series, about $50 to $150

cards.head: Magnetic base
cards.text: Articulating, with fine adjustment; for example Noga MG71003 or DG-61003, about $140 to $320

cards.head: Steel base plate
cards.text: About 150 x 100 x 12 mm, bolted to the cell table with two M8 screws, so the base holds on a non-magnetic table and does not creep

cards.head: Placement
cards.text: Where the indicator tip reaches the board's front face about 20 mm from an edge with the robot in its run-out pose

slides.caption: The run-out check: the flange turns, the indicator stays still, the reading must stay within 0.05 mm.
slides.notes: The run-out check in deck 2 needs the dial indicator held still while the robot turns the board about the flange axis. A magnetic base alone can creep or fail to hold on an aluminum or stone table, so it stands on a small steel plate bolted to the table. All three items are stocked by McMaster-Carr and the usual tool suppliers. The fixture needs no drawing beyond the plate's size and its two bolt holes.

slides.title: A stiff, repeatable chain from flange to sphere
slides.caption: Adapter on the flange's dowel, with the stem's shoulder seated on the adapter face.
points: Adapter located by the flange dowel, so a remount lands in the same place
Ground 30 mm stem keeps sag to about 0.05 mm
Stem length at least 2R + 50 mm, so the sphere hides the stem
Witness mark across stem and adapter shows a loosened joint
After any remount, re-check in the nest: readings within 0.1 mm
slides.notes: Where the sphere center ends up does not need to be known from drawings, because the tool-center-point routine measures it; what matters is that it does not move afterwards. The adapter plate's mounting face, outer face and tapped hole are machined in one lathe setup, located on the flange pilot, so the hole is perpendicular to the face within 0.02 mm over 100 mm. The stem is deliberately thick: a 25 mm stem would let the sphere sag about 0.1 mm, and that sag would change with the robot's orientation. The shoulder on the stem, machined square in the same setup as its thread, sets the stem perpendicular to the adapter. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-02 adapter plate, SC1-04 stem with the sphere interface, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base (SC1-01 and SC1-03, for the former second sphere, are archived). The adapter plate is 63 mm across and 22 mm thick, with a 31.5 mm centering spigot and one 6 mm dowel for the ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6 flange.

slides.title: The sphere end: thread cut at the pole, or a bonded stem
slides.label: Aluminum sphere B: thread cut at the pole
slides.label2: Steel or ceramic alternative: bonded blind hole
slides.caption: The hole need not be exactly radial: the tool-center-point routine measures the center wherever it ends up.
slides.notes: The turned aluminum sphere has an M20 x 30 mm hole tapped at a pole, with a 32 mm spot face, cut in the same setup in which it is turned. The stem's M20 tip threads in and its end seats on the spot face, with a drop of medium-strength thread locker. Only if the sphere is bought in steel or ceramic does the bonded alternative apply: hardened spheres cannot be tapped, so a shop makes a blind hole 16 H7 by 46 mm by carbide drilling or electrical discharge machining, sized for a light press fit, and the stem is bonded in with anaerobic retaining compound. Never weld or braze: the heat distorts the sphere. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-02 adapter plate, SC1-04 stem with the sphere interface, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base (SC1-01 and SC1-03, for the former second sphere, are archived).

slides.title: The board must stay flat after finishing and mounting
slides.caption: Board on its adapter. The runout and frame checks shown here are done at setup (deck 2).

cards.head: Plate
cards.text: 200 x 150 mm, at least 6 mm thick; ground aluminum tooling plate or float glass

cards.head: Finish
cards.text: Matte light gray paint on the front face; do not bead-blast a plate thinner than about 10 mm, it bows

cards.head: Flatness
cards.text: 0.05 mm, checked after painting and mounting, not before; keep the flatness report

cards.head: Adapter
cards.text: Three support pads, three edge pins and three clamp fingers hold the board square to the flange axis, centered on it, and in the same place after a remount

slides.notes: Thickness is not a stiffness question: a 6 mm plate sags only about 0.002 mm under its own weight. It only has to survive the finish and the mounting flat. Bead-blasting peens one face and bows a thin plate, so paint over the ground or glass surface instead. Flatness is checked last, after painting and mounting, because that is the state the sensor sees; the flatness report is also the reference for the board-flatness check in the validation. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-02 adapter plate, SC1-04 stem with the sphere interface, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base (SC1-01 and SC1-03, for the former second sphere, are archived).

slides.title: A three-ball nest holds the sphere at a fixed center
points: Three hardened balls, 24 mm diameter, bonded into pockets on a 60 mm circle in a 120 mm steel base
Ordinary grade-25 bearing balls are good enough: the nest's quality comes from the balls being rigidly fixed
Bolted to the table where the robot reaches with the wrist down and tilted about 40 degrees to either side
Used once at setup, and after any remount of the adapter or stem
slides.notes: A sphere resting on three fixed balls always has its center at the same point in space, whatever direction its stem points. That is what lets the robot's own multi-orientation routine find the sphere's center as its tool center point, which deck 2 describes. The nest is simple to make: a steel base with three pockets, the balls bonded in, and holes to bolt it down. Its position matters only in that the robot must be able to seat the sphere from several directions. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-02 adapter plate, SC1-04 stem with the sphere interface, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base (SC1-01 and SC1-03, for the former second sphere, are archived).

slides.title: Checks before the fixtures go to the robot cell
checklist: Fabricator's inspection report received for the sphere and for SC1-02, SC1-04, SC1-05 and SC1-06
Sphere matte, uniform and free of highlights
Sphere diameter and sphericity by micrometer after finishing: spread within 0.02 mm, temperature recorded
Board flat to 0.05 mm by straightedge and feeler leaf, after painting and mounting
Board width and length measured with calipers
At setup (deck 2): board run-out within 0.05 mm on the robot; nest re-seat within 0.1 mm
Each fixture weighed for its tool load data; witness mark across the stem-adapter joint
slides.notes: These are the only checks made in-house (decision D-18 of the analysis); every toleranced feature of the machined parts and of the sphere is in the fabricators' inspection reports, which are the as-built record. Each check protects something the software cannot repair later: a shiny spot gives bad reads, an unmeasured diameter or a bowed board puts a wrong reference into every observation, and a board face that is not square to the flange tilts every board pose. The run-out reading checks only that squareness; it cannot see a dished face, which is why flatness is checked with the straightedge. The fixture weights feed the robot's tool load data, which its absolute accuracy depends on. The dimensioned shop drawings are in appendix D of the stage-1 procedure, and as PNG files in docs/procedures/drawings/ of the repository: SC1-02 adapter plate, SC1-04 stem with the sphere interface, SC1-05 board adapter, SC1-06 nest base (SC1-01 and SC1-03, for the former second sphere, are archived).
